generatedProse.concept-context: Academic tasks rarely have one right route. A report can be structured in several ways, a question approached with different methods, a problem framed through more than one idea. Thinking flexibly means producing a few of these approaches before you commit, then watching how your chosen approach goes. If it stalls, you amend it or switch, rather than forcing a structure that is not working.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students are set the same demanding task with a tight deadline.

{{learner-a}} picks the first structure that comes to mind and commits to it. Half way through, the sections clearly do not hang together, but {{learner-a}} pushes on the same way, hoping more effort will fix it. Time runs out with little to show. There was never a second structure to turn to.

{{learner-b}} starts by jotting three ways the task could be organised, then tries the most promising one. Watching the argument stall, {{learner-b}} stops, returns to the list, and switches to a structure that fits the material better. The task gets finished, because a change of course was always available.

Both students worked hard. Only {{learner-b}} generated options and stayed ready to adapt, turning a stall into a switch rather than a dead end.
generatedProse.summary: Thinking flexibly has two parts: generating several approaches to a task before you commit, and monitoring your chosen approach so you can adapt or switch when it is not working. You can now produce more than one way into a task, watch how an approach is going, and change course with control rather than pushing on regardless. The next lesson turns creativity onto the material itself, bringing imagination to analysis.

check.body: In the worked example, what let {{learner-b}} realise the first approach was not working?

items.text: {{learner-b}} kept checking, while working, whether the structure was getting anywhere.
{{learner-b}} waited until the deadline to review the whole task.
{{learner-b}} had chosen only one structure from the start.

feedback.correct: That's right. Monitoring the work while going is what let {{learner-b}} spot the stall in time to switch.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. What was {{learner-b}} doing while working that {{learner-a}} was not?
